inputs.original_text: A Wisconsin jury found Harry Wait guilty of two misdemeanor election fraud charges and one felony identity theft charge after he requested ballots for Republican Assembly Speaker Robin Vos and Democratic Racine Mayor Cory Mason without their consent. He was acquitted of a second identity theft count. Wait said he wanted to expose vulnerabilities in the voter registration system, but manufacturing fraud is not a legitimate way to protect democracy. And this case is not evidence of widespread voter fraud: it shows how false election claims can damage public trust. We need secure, accessible election systems and accountability for people who undermine them—not excuses to restrict ordinary people’s right to vote.
inputs.modified_text: Harry Wait was found guilty of two misdemeanor election fraud charges and one felony identity theft charge after requesting ballots for Robin Vos and Cory Mason without their consent, though he was acquitted of another identity theft count. His claim that he was exposing vulnerabilities doesn’t excuse manufacturing fraud—but neither does this case justify making voting harder for ordinary people. The real danger is turning isolated misconduct into an excuse to undermine public trust or restrict access. We need election systems that are both secure and accessible, and accountability that protects voters rather than punishing them.
